title: Polynesian
description: Not one mythology but a family of them, spread across a triangle bigger than Eurasia - kept by island group, because the names travelled and the meanings did not.
sources: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855) - Maori accounts taken from named tohunga
Elsdon Best, The Maori (1924) and related monographs
David Malo, Hawaiian Antiquities (c. 1840) and Samuel Kamakau - Hawaiian scholars writing in Hawaiian
Martha Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (1940) and her translation of the Kumulipo (1951)
Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928), from her grandfather's manuscripts
Note: Maori and Hawaiian traditions are living. Particular iwi and families hold their own versions; this is the published record and no version is presented as the correct one
portraitNote: Portraits are original illustrations in a single uniform style for the whole pack, stored locally in the portraits/polynesian/ folder. No images are fetched from the network.

kumulipo.t: The Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant

profile.cosmicNature: Usually a growth rather than a making. The Hawaiian Kumulipo begins in darkness and works upward through coral, then worms, then fish, then birds, then people, in a chant of two thousand lines that is essentially a genealogy of everything. In Aotearoa the sky and the earth are locked together in an embrace and their children are crushed between them until one of them forces the two apart. In Tahiti, Ta'aroa sits alone inside a shell and eventually breaks it and uses the pieces.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Four great gods in most of the ocean, and beyond them a genealogy that runs continuously from the gods to living people. Tane or Kane, Tu or Ku, Rongo or Lono, Tangaroa or Kanaloa - the same four names, in different orders of seniority depending which island you ask. Below them are ancestors, who are not separate from gods in kind, only in distance, and the boundary between the two is a matter of how many generations back.
profile.afterlife: West, and down, and along a specific road. In Aotearoa the spirit travels north to Te Rerenga Wairua, the leaping place at the top of the island, climbs down a root of the pohutukawa tree and goes to Rarohenga. In Hawaii it goes to a leina, a leaping place, on each island. In much of the ocean the dead go towards Pulotu or Hawaiki - the homeland, which is also where the living came from, so the dead are going back rather than going away.
profile.systemMechanism: Mana and tapu, and they are a pair. Mana is effective power - in a person, an object, a place, a chief - and it can be gained, inherited, and lost. Tapu is restriction: what is charged with mana is set apart and cannot be treated ordinarily, and violating it is dangerous whether or not anyone intends harm. Noa is the ordinary state, and there are procedures for moving things from one to the other. The English word taboo comes from this and lost most of the meaning on the way.
profile.canonTexts: Nothing written before contact. What exists is very large: Maori accounts recorded from named tohunga in the nineteenth century, above all by George Grey and later by Elsdon Best and Ngata; the Hawaiian material collected by David Malo, Samuel Kamakau and Abraham Fornander, all Hawaiian; the Kumulipo itself, a two-thousand-line creation chant preserved by chiefly families; and Teuira Henry's Tahitian material from her missionary grandfather's notes.

hierarchy.title: Across the Ocean
hierarchy.blurb: The names that travelled the whole triangle. Four great gods - Tane, Tu, Rongo, Tangaroa - who change rank from island to island. Hina, who is in the moon beating tapa nearly everywhere. And Maui, the youngest brother who fished up islands and slowed the sun and got away with it.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: In the south, they are all children of a couple who would not let go of each other

hierarchy.title: Aotearoa
hierarchy.blurb: The sky and the earth lie locked together and their children grow up crushed in the dark between them, until one of them lies on his back and pushes. The rain afterwards is the father crying. And Maui dies here, which he does nowhere else, trying to end death.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Three thousand miles north, the same four gods and an entirely different story

hierarchy.title: Hawaii
hierarchy.blurb: Pele dug a home on each island in turn from Kauai southeast and the sea flooded every one until she reached Hawaii - which is the actual geological history of the chain, in the correct order. She is not a goddess of the volcano. She is the lava.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: In the middle of the triangle, a creator who had nothing at all to work with

hierarchy.title: Tahiti
hierarchy.blurb: Ta'aroa sat alone inside a shell in the dark with no sky, no sea and nobody to call to. When he broke out he used one half of the shell for the sky and the other for the ground, and made everything else out of his own body because there was nothing else.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: West again, where the first people came out of a rotting vine

hierarchy.title: Samoa & Tonga
hierarchy.blurb: Tagaloa threw a rock into the empty sea to have somewhere to stand. A war goddess fought with her chest bound and stopped when the wind exposed her. And an eel that loved a girl asked her to bury its head, which is why a coconut has a face.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: And at the far corner, the most isolated inhabited place on earth

hierarchy.title: Rapa Nui
hierarchy.blurb: Two thousand kilometres from the nearest inhabited island, found on purpose because a priest dreamed it. When the ancestor cult of the moai ended, it was replaced by an annual swim through shark water to fetch the first tern egg of the season.

stories.title: Pushing With His Legs
stories.summary: Ranginui and Papatuanuku held each other so closely that their children grew up between them in total darkness, unable to stand upright. The children argued about it. Tumatauenga proposed killing them. The others preferred separation, and tried in turn - Rongo, Tangaroa, Haumia, Tu - and none of them could shift it. Then Tane put his shoulders against his mother and his feet against his father and straightened his legs, slowly, and they came apart, and light came in for the first time. Tawhirimatea, the only one who had objected, went up with his father and made war on his brothers ever afterwards. And Ranginui grieves: the rain is him weeping down, and the mist that lifts off the land at dawn is Papatuanuku's grief going back up to him.

sources.location: The Children of Heaven and Earth

stories.title: Beating the Sun Until It Slowed Down
stories.summary: The days were too short. The sun went over too fast, and there was not enough light to get the work done or to cook properly, and in the Hawaiian telling Maui's mother Hina could not get her tapa dry. So Maui and his brothers plaited ropes - flax in the south, coconut fibre elsewhere - and went east and waited at the pit the sun rises from, and when it came up they dropped the nooses over it and held on and beat it with the jawbone until it agreed to move more slowly for part of the year. In Hawaii this happens at Haleakala, which means the house of the sun, and it is a real mountain you can drive up. It is a story about the working day, and every version of it is.

stories.title: The Fantail Laughed
stories.summary: Maui had done everything else, and decided to end death. Hine-nui-te-po lay asleep at the horizon, enormous, with eyes of flashing greenstone and teeth of obsidian, and he intended to pass through her body and out of her mouth, which would reverse the direction of birth and make people deathless. He told the birds who came with him that whatever they saw, they must not make a sound until he was through. He went in. The little fantail, watching, could not hold it, and laughed out loud. She woke, and closed on him, and that was the end of Maui and the end of the possibility. It is the reason people die, and the reason is that somebody could not keep a straight face.

stories.title: Digging Down the Island Chain
stories.summary: Pele came from Kahiki in a canoe, driven out and pursued by her elder sister Namaka, who is the sea. She landed on Kauai, at the northwestern end of the chain, and dug for a home, and the sea came in and flooded the pit. So she moved southeast to Oahu, and dug, and it flooded. Then Molokai, then Maui, each one further southeast and each one flooded, until she reached the island of Hawaii and dug Halemaumau on Kilauea, which is high enough and new enough and far enough east that her sister cannot reach it. She is there now. That sequence - northwest to southeast, older to younger - is the exact order in which the Hawaiian islands were formed as the plate moved over a stationary hotspot.

stories.title: Alone Inside the Shell
stories.summary: Ta'aroa existed in a shell, in the dark, rolling about in a void, and there was no sky, no land, no sea, no sand, and nobody anywhere to call out to. He called out anyway and nothing answered. So he broke the shell and stood on it, and made another shell over himself, and eventually used one for the dome of the sky and the other for the ground and the rocks. Then, having no material of any kind, he made the rest of the world from his own body: his feathers became the trees and the creepers, his flesh the fat soil, his bones the ridges of the mountains, his entrails the eels and the lobsters, his blood the red in the sky at sunset and the colour of the rainbow. Then he made other gods and gave them the rest of the work.

stories.title: Maggots in a Rotting Vine
stories.summary: Tagaloa stood in the sky when there was nothing below but sea, and threw down a rock so that he would have somewhere to put his feet, and that was the first land. He sent down a creeping vine to shade it. The vine grew and spread and then withered and rotted, and maggots bred in the rot, and Tagaloa sent his messenger down to them - and the messenger split each maggot and gave it arms and legs and a heart and a mind, and they stood up as the first people. It is one of the least flattering origins any people has given itself, and Samoan tradition tells it without apology and is entirely specific about which rock and which islands.

stories.title: Why the Coconut Has a Face
stories.summary: Sina kept a small eel in a pool and fed it, and it grew, and it turned out to be a young chief from another island under an enchantment, and it began to follow her about and to look at her in a way she did not like. She ran, and it followed - pool to pool, village to village, across the islands. In the end it was caught and killed, and its dying request was that its head be buried, and Sina did that. A palm grew out of the buried head. When you husk a coconut there are three marks on the shell, two eyes and a mouth, and to drink from it you have to put your own mouth against the eel's, which is what the whole story was built to arrive at.

stories.title: Swimming for the First Egg
stories.summary: Every spring the clans gathered at Orongo on the cliff top, and each competitor sent a servant down the rock face, into the sea, and out across a kilometre and a half of shark water to the islet of Motu Nui - on a bundle of reeds - to wait for the sooty terns to nest. They waited in caves, sometimes for weeks. The first man to find an egg shouted his sponsor's name across the water, tied the egg to his forehead, swam back, and climbed the cliff, and men died doing both. His sponsor became tangata manu for a year: head and eyebrows shaved, painted, housed apart, under heavy restriction and holding real authority. It replaced the moai-building ancestor cult entirely, and the last competition was held around 1867.

stories.title: Forty Days to Kauai
stories.summary: Pele saw a man named Lohiau in a dream on Kauai and sent her youngest sister to fetch him, with two conditions: be back in forty days, and do not embrace him. Hiiaka went the length of the island chain and had to fight moo and sorcerers the whole way, and when she reached Kauai Lohiau was dead, and reviving him took days more. On the way back the forty days ran out. Pele, waiting, assumed the worst and burned Hiiaka's lehua groves, and then killed Lohiau. Hiiaka began digging down toward the fire pit. The epic runs to hundreds of pages, was serialised in the Hawaiian-language newspapers in the nineteenth century, and is where the hula tradition keeps its charter.

stories.title: Coral First
stories.summary: The Kumulipo runs to about two thousand lines and begins in the deep darkness before anything. The first living thing born in it is the coral polyp. After the coral come the sea creatures, and each one is paired with a plant of the land that shares something with its name - the sea cucumber with the sweet potato, and so on down a very long list. Then worms and shellfish, then fish, then insects, then birds, then reptiles, then the mammals, and only then people - and from there the chant continues without a break into the genealogy of a particular chiefly line, which is the point of the whole thing. Queen Liliuokalani translated it into English while imprisoned in her own palace after the overthrow of 1893.

sources.book: The Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant

entities.name: Maui
entities.role: He fished up islands, slowed the sun, stole fire, and died trying to end death
symbols: the jawbone of his ancestress, used as a hook
entities.bio: He is the most widely known figure in the Pacific, and he is a younger brother getting away with things.
entities.longBio: Maui is told from Aotearoa to Hawaii to Tonga to Tahiti and the same things happen to him nearly everywhere. He is the youngest, born prematurely and thrown into the sea wrapped in his mother's topknot, and rescued. He beats the sun with a noose until it agrees to move slower so there is time to get work done. He fishes up land with a hook made from his ancestress's jawbone, and his brothers cut into the fish while it is still thrashing, which is why the country is mountainous. He gets fire out of Mahuika by asking for her fingernails one at a time. He is a younger sibling who wins by cheek, and the ocean found that funny for three thousand years.
entities.variantTraditions: Only the Maori tradition kills him. In Hawaii and Tahiti he simply stops appearing, and in Tonga he is chiefly the fisher-up of islands.

entities.name: Tangaroa
entities.role: The sea - except in Tahiti, where he made everything, and in Hawaii, where he ended up a demon
entities.bio: The same name is the sea god, the creator, and a banished spirit, depending which island you stand on.
entities.longBio: Tangaroa is the clearest single demonstration of why these traditions should not be merged. In Aotearoa he is the sea, one of the sons of Rangi and Papa, and the ancestor of fish, and he is on bad terms with his brother Tane because Tane sheltered the reptiles that should have gone into the water. In Tahiti, as Ta'aroa, he is the creator of everything and sits alone in a shell before the world exists. In Samoa, as Tagaloa, he is likewise the supreme creator. In Hawaii, as Kanaloa, he is one of the four great gods and in some later accounts becomes a rebel and something close to an adversary.
entities.variantTraditions: The Hawaiian demotion of Kanaloa toward a devil figure may be partly a missionary-era development, and this is argued about.

entities.name: Tane
entities.role: The forest, the light, and the one who made the first woman out of earth
domains: the making of the first woman
entities.bio: He forced his parents apart by lying on his back and pushing with his legs.
entities.longBio: Tane is the forest and everything in it, and in the Maori account he is the one who ended the darkness: with the sky and the earth locked together and their children crushed between them, his brothers tried to force them apart and failed, and Tane lay on his back and pushed with his legs and shoulders until Rangi went up and Papa stayed down and there was light. He then went up through the heavens for the three baskets of knowledge. Wanting a wife and finding no women, he made one out of red earth at Kurawaka and breathed into her nostrils, and she was Hine-ahu-one. In Hawaii, as Kane, he is the senior of the four great gods.
entities.variantTraditions: In Hawaii Kane is associated with fresh water and sunlight and heads the four; the tree and forest emphasis is stronger in the south.

entities.name: Tu
entities.role: War, and the only brother who was willing to fight his own family
entities.bio: When his brothers would not fight, he set about eating all of them, which is why people eat everything.
entities.longBio: Tumatauenga wanted to kill his parents outright rather than separate them, and was overruled. Then, when his brother Tawhirimatea attacked the others and they hid or fled, Tu was the only one who stood and fought him, and won. Afterwards he took revenge on the brothers who had not helped: he snared Tane's birds, netted Tangaroa's fish, dug up Rongo and Haumia's crops, and ate all of them. That is the charter for human beings eating everything in the world and for the ritual of cooking, which removes tapu. He is humanity's own ancestor and he is not presented as admirable.
entities.variantTraditions: In Hawaii, Ku is one of the four great gods and receives the most serious offerings; the Maori Tu is not a supreme figure but a brother.

entities.name: Rongo
entities.role: Cultivated food and peace, and in Hawaii his festival stopped all war for four months
symbols: the long white banner of the Makahiki
entities.bio: The Hawaiian Makahiki ran four months, during which fighting was forbidden and taxes were collected.
entities.longBio: Rongo is the cultivated food - the kumara above all - and by extension peace, since the two go together. In Hawaii, as Lono, he governs rain and agriculture and the Makahiki, a festival running about four months from the rising of the Pleiades, during which war was prohibited, work was reduced, tribute was collected and there were games. Captain Cook arrived off Hawaii during the Makahiki in 1779, at the right season and sailing round the island in the right direction, and what was made of that at the time is still argued about by historians.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Cook was taken for Lono, and in what sense, is one of the more heated disputes in Pacific anthropology.

entities.name: Hina
entities.role: The most widespread woman in the Pacific, and usually she is in the moon beating tapa
entities.bio: She got fed up with her family, took her calabash and her tapa beater and went to the moon.
entities.longBio: Hina appears in more islands than any other female figure and is not always the same person - she is Maui's mother in some traditions and his sister or wife in others, and in yet others she has nothing to do with him. The most widespread story has her tired of her life, or of her husband, taking her tapa-beating board and her calabash and climbing to the moon, where she can be seen. In Samoa, Sina is the girl an eel fell in love with; when it was killed she buried the head as instructed, and the first coconut grew, which is why the nut has a face on it.
entities.variantTraditions: The Sina and the eel origin of the coconut is Samoan and Tongan; the woman in the moon beating tapa is nearly pan-Polynesian.

entities.name: Ranginui
entities.role: The sky, who held his wife so tightly that their children lived in the dark
symbols: the rain, which is his weeping
the mist rising, which is hers
entities.bio: The rain is him still crying, and the mist that rises off the ground is her answering.
entities.longBio: Ranginui and Papatuanuku lay locked together and their children were born and grew between them in complete darkness, cramped and unable to stand. The children debated what to do - Tumatauenga wanted to kill them, the others wanted them separated - and one after another they tried to push and failed, until Tane lay on his back and forced them apart with his legs. Rangi went up. He grieves for her constantly: the rain is his tears falling, and the mist that rises off the land in the morning is her grief going up to him. It is one of the few separation myths anywhere where the point is that the separation hurt.
entities.variantTraditions: The version best known is Grey's, from Te Rangikaheke of Ngati Rangiwewehi. Other iwi tell it differently, including the number of children.

entities.name: Papatuanuku
entities.role: The earth, and everyone who lives on her is living on their mother
domains: the dead who return to her
symbols: the placenta, which is buried in the land
entities.bio: Whenua is the Maori word for both land and placenta, and the placenta is buried in the ground.
entities.longBio: Papatuanuku is the earth and she is not a metaphor for it. The word whenua means both land and afterbirth, and a child's placenta is buried in the ground of the family's land, which puts the person and the place in the same relationship as the mother and the child. When Tane forced her apart from Rangi she was turned face down so that she would not have to look at him, and the mist rising in the morning is her grief. The dead go back into her. Everything that grows is hers, and the argument that land can be owned and sold ran directly into this.
entities.variantTraditions: The turning of Papa face down is in some accounts and not others; the whenua-placenta practice is general and continues.

entities.name: Tawhirimatea
entities.role: The winds, and the only son who took his parents' side and never forgave the others
symbols: the winds of the four quarters
entities.bio: He is said to have torn out his own eyes and thrown them into the sky, where they are the Pleiades.
entities.longBio: Tawhirimatea alone opposed separating the parents, and when it was done anyway he went up with his father and made war on his brothers. He drove Tane's forests flat, chased Tangaroa's fish into the sea and his reptiles into the bush, flattened Rongo and Haumia's crops so that they had to hide in the earth, and only Tumatauenga stood and fought him. In one much-repeated account he was so angry that he tore out his own eyes, crushed them and flung them into the sky, where they became Matariki, the Pleiades, whose rising marks the Maori new year - which is now a public holiday in New Zealand.
entities.variantTraditions: The eyes-into-Matariki account is one telling among several and has become widely known since Matariki was made a national holiday in 2022.

entities.name: Hine-nui-te-po
entities.role: The great woman of the night, who killed Maui and so kept death in the world
symbols: the red of the sunset where she waits
entities.abode: The far horizon, at the entrance to the night
entities.bio: Maui tried to reverse birth by entering her while she slept. A bird laughed, she woke, and he died.
entities.longBio: Hine-nui-te-po was Hine-titama, the dawn maiden, until she discovered that her husband Tane was also her father, and fled to the underworld in shame and grief, and told him to stay above and raise their children while she pulled them down. She became the goddess of death. Maui, meaning to end death for everyone, went to her while she slept, intending to pass through her body and reverse the direction of birth. He told the birds with him to keep silent. The little fantail could not, and laughed, and she woke, and he was crushed, and because he failed people have died ever since.
entities.variantTraditions: Different iwi tell the ending differently and some regard the detail as not for general recounting; the summary here follows the published Grey and Best accounts.

entities.name: Hine-titama
entities.role: The dawn maiden, who asked who her father was and got an answer she could not live with
symbols: the children she called after her
entities.abode: The dawn, and then the underworld
entities.bio: She asked her husband who her father was. He would not answer, so she asked the doorposts.
entities.longBio: Tane made the first woman out of red earth and then took their daughter Hine-titama as his wife, and she did not know. When she asked him who her father was he told her to ask the posts of the house, which was an answer, and she understood it. She went down to Rarohenga and would not come back, and when Tane followed she told him to go up and stay in the world of light and raise their children, and that she would remain below and draw them down to her when their time came. She stopped being the dawn and became the night, and that is where death comes from in this tradition.
entities.variantTraditions: The transformation of Hine-titama into Hine-nui-te-po is standard; the treatment of Tane's part varies considerably between iwi.

entities.name: Ruaumoko
entities.role: The unborn child still inside his mother, and when he turns over there is an earthquake
entities.bio: New Zealand sits on a plate boundary, and this is the explanation that fits it exactly.
entities.longBio: When Papatuanuku was turned face down, her youngest son had not yet been born and was still inside her, and he is there now. When he moves the ground shakes and the mountains smoke. In some accounts he was given fire to keep his mother warm, which is the volcanoes, and his movement through the year makes the seasons. Aotearoa sits directly on the boundary between two plates and has thousands of earthquakes a year and a line of active volcanoes down the middle of the North Island, and a myth of a restless unborn child inside the earth is an extremely good fit for the evidence available.
entities.variantTraditions: Also given as Ruamoko. The seasonal explanation is one strand; the earthquake association is universal.

entities.name: Tawhaki
entities.role: He climbed to the top of the sky on a vine, and lightning comes off him
symbols: the vine or the line of spider thread
entities.bio: He was beaten and left for dead by his wife's brothers, and went up to get what he needed.
entities.longBio: Tawhaki is beautiful, is beaten nearly to death by his jealous brothers-in-law, recovers, and climbs to the heavens - up a vine, or a line of spider silk, or the tendril of a creeper, depending on the telling - to reach the topmost sky and the knowledge kept there. Lightning flashes from his armpits when he moves. He is one of the very few figures whose story travelled the whole triangle with the name recognisably intact: Kaha'i in Hawaii, Tafa'i in Tahiti, Tahaki in the Tuamotus, doing more or less the same things in each.
entities.variantTraditions: The ascent to the heavens and the lightning are constant; the reason for the climb varies between recovering a wife, a child, and knowledge.

entities.name: Kupe
entities.role: The navigator who found Aotearoa, chasing an octopus that had been stealing his bait
epithets: the one who came from Hawaiki
entities.bio: His wife is said to have seen the land and called it a long white cloud - Aotearoa.
entities.longBio: Kupe is the navigator who found Aotearoa, and the story given for the voyage is domestic rather than epic: a giant octopus belonging to a man named Muturangi kept stripping the bait off his fishing lines, and he went after it, and the chase took him across the ocean. He killed it in Cook Strait. His wife Kuramarotini, seeing land ahead, is said to have called out about a long white cloud, and Aotearoa is usually explained from that. He named a great many places, went back to Hawaiki with the sailing directions, and did not return - and that is what made the later migration possible.
entities.variantTraditions: Kupe traditions differ substantially between iwi, and several regions hold their own accounts of who arrived and when. There is no single agreed version.

entities.name: Taniwha
entities.role: A creature in a river or a harbour that may guard you or may eat you
epithets: the one in the deep water
symbols: the log that is not a log
entities.abode: A particular pool, reef, cave or stretch of coast
entities.bio: Some are kaitiaki, guardians of a hapu; others simply take people, and the distinction is local.
entities.longBio: A taniwha lives in a specific place - a pool, a bend of a river, a reef, a stretch of harbour - and it is not a species so much as an individual with a name and a relationship to a particular hapu. Some are guardians who warn of danger and escort canoes; others are dangerous and have to be killed by a hero. The practical function is unmistakable, since taniwha are consistently located exactly where the water is treacherous. They remain a live matter in New Zealand: taniwha have been cited in resource-consent and roading cases, and courts have had to decide what to do about it.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether a given taniwha is a guardian or a menace depends entirely on which hapu is speaking and which taniwha it is.

entities.name: Io
entities.role: A supreme being above all the others - and scholars are genuinely unsure whether he is old
symbols: the name that was not spoken
entities.bio: The dispute is real and unresolved, and pretending otherwise would be the dishonest thing here.
entities.longBio: Io is described as the supreme being, parentless, existing before everything, whose name was known only to the highest tohunga and taught only in the whare wananga. He appears in material recorded in the later nineteenth century, particularly through Elsdon Best and Te Matorohanga. The question is whether he is an ancient esoteric tradition that was simply never told to outsiders before, or a figure shaped in response to Christian monotheism during a period of intense missionary pressure. Serious scholars, including Maori scholars, have argued both, and the matter is not settled.
entities.variantTraditions: This entry deliberately does not decide. The argument runs from Best onwards and the evidence genuinely permits both readings.

entities.name: Pele
entities.role: The volcano - not a goddess of it, the thing itself, and she is currently at Kilauea
epithets: Pelehonuamea, Pele of the sacred earth
Ka wahine ai honua, the woman who eats the land
symbols: the white dog seen before an eruption
entities.bio: Offerings are still left at the crater rim, and this is not a folk survival - it is current.
entities.longBio: Pele came from Kahiki by canoe, pursued by her elder sister Namaka the sea, and dug for a home on each island in turn from Kauai down the chain, and each time the sea flooded her pit, until she reached Hawaii and dug Halemaumau, which is high enough and far enough east. That sequence is the actual geological history of the archipelago in the correct order - the islands are progressively younger to the southeast, because the plate moves over a fixed hotspot - and the tradition had it right. She is not a goddess who governs volcanoes; the lava is her. Offerings are left at the crater today.
entities.variantTraditions: The Pele and Hiiaka epic is enormous, was published in Hawaiian-language newspapers at length, and is one of the great bodies of Pacific literature.

entities.name: Hiiaka
entities.role: Pele's youngest sister, sent on an errand that took months and ended in fire
epithets: Hiiaka-i-ka-poli-o-Pele, Hiiaka in the bosom of Pele
entities.abode: Kilauea, and the road across the islands
entities.bio: She was given forty days to fetch Pele's lover from Kauai and told not to touch him.
entities.longBio: Pele sent her youngest sister to Kauai to fetch the man she wanted, Lohiau, with two conditions: forty days, and no embracing him. The journey took far longer, because Hiiaka had to fight her way through moo - lizard spirits - and sorcerers the whole length of the chain, and when she arrived Lohiau was dead and she had to bring him back to life, which took days. Pele, waiting and suspicious, burned Hiiaka's beloved lehua groves and then killed Lohiau. Hiiaka dug down toward the fire pit in fury. The epic is very long, was serialised in Hawaiian newspapers, and is where the hula tradition locates itself.
entities.variantTraditions: Multiple versions were published by different authors between the 1860s and 1920s and they differ in emphasis and in the ending.

entities.name: Namaka
entities.role: The sea, and Pele's elder sister, who chased her the entire length of the islands
symbols: the wave that floods a new crater
entities.bio: Every time Pele dug a pit, her sister flooded it - which is what the sea does to a new vent.
entities.longBio: Namaka is the sea and Pele's elder sister, and the quarrel between them - over a husband, in most accounts - is why Pele left home and why she could not settle. Each island Pele dug into, from Kauai southeast, Namaka flooded, until Pele got far enough east and high enough on Hawaii to be out of reach. They fought physically on Maui and Pele was torn apart, and her body is a hill there while her spirit went on to Kilauea. Sea against new lava is the single most visible process on that coast, and the story is a precise account of it.
entities.variantTraditions: The fight at Kahikinui on Maui and the hill called Pele's bones are located specifically in the tradition.

entities.name: Kamapuaa
entities.role: A pig demigod, half man and half hog, who fought Pele to a draw and divided the island with her
epithets: the one with eight eyes in some chants
entities.abode: The windward side of the island, where it is wet
entities.bio: Fire against rain, fought to a standstill, so they split the island between them.
entities.longBio: Kamapuaa is a demigod who takes the form of a hog, a handsome man, several plants and a fish, and he is a thief and a seducer and extremely difficult to kill. He came to Pele and they insulted each other at length in chant, and then fought - fire against water and rain - and neither could destroy the other. So they divided Hawaii: the dry leeward side, where the lava is, went to Pele, and the wet windward side to Kamapuaa. That division is the actual rainfall map of the island. Their exchange of insults is one of the more scabrous things in the published Hawaiian record.
entities.variantTraditions: Beckwith and Fornander both give versions; the chanted insult contest survives in several forms.

entities.name: Poliahu
entities.role: The snow goddess of Mauna Kea, and Pele's other enemy
epithets: the snow maiden of Mauna Kea
entities.bio: Hawaii has snow, on a mountain higher than anything in the continental United States west of it.
entities.longBio: Poliahu lives on the summit of Mauna Kea, which is a shade under 4,200 metres and does get snow, and she wears white kapa. She and Pele are enemies, which is a straightforward statement about a single island holding both an active lava lake and a snowfield, and the fights between them are described as snow advancing down the mountain against lava coming up it. She raced sleds against Pele in one story, on the grass slopes, and won, and Pele broke the ground open under her. Mauna Kea remains among the most contested sacred sites in Hawaii.
entities.variantTraditions: Her sisters Lilinoe and Waiau are also associated with the summit; Lake Waiau near the top is named for one of them.

entities.name: Laka
entities.role: Hula - which is not entertainment but a way of keeping the record
epithets: the one of the forest greenery
symbols: the maile and lehua on the altar
entities.abode: The hula school, and the forest it takes its greenery from
entities.bio: Missionaries banned it in 1830; it survived because it was how things were remembered.
entities.longBio: Laka is the goddess of hula and of the forest plants used in it, and her altar in a halau is dressed with greenery gathered with chant and permission. Hula in the old sense is not a performance but a memory system - genealogies, place names, histories and prayers held in chant and rendered by the body, in a society with no writing. The Calvinist mission had it banned in 1830, and it was performed quietly for decades and revived publicly under Kalakaua in the 1880s, and has been fully restored since the 1970s. It is one of the clearest cases anywhere of an art form being load-bearing.
entities.variantTraditions: Laka is also a male figure in some traditions - a canoe-maker and voyager - and the two are probably unrelated despite the shared name.

entities.name: Haumea
entities.role: Childbirth, and she could make herself young again and marry her own descendants
symbols: the breadfruit tree she turned into
entities.bio: She is credited with teaching women to give birth in the ordinary way rather than by being cut open.
entities.longBio: Haumea is the mother of Pele and of a great many others, and she is a goddess of childbirth and wild growing food. Her distinguishing feature is that she can renew herself: she becomes young again repeatedly and marries her own descendants down the generations, so the genealogy loops. She is credited with a specific intervention - teaching women to give birth naturally, where before, in the tradition, children had to be cut out and the mother died. When pursued she stepped into a breadfruit tree and it closed over her. She is one of the oldest and least tidy figures in the Hawaiian record.
entities.variantTraditions: Haumea is identified with Papa, the earth, in some chants and kept separate in others; Beckwith treats the identification as secondary.

entities.name: The Kumulipo
entities.role: A two-thousand-line chant that starts in the dark with coral and works up to people
symbols: the coral polyp, first of all
entities.bio: It pairs every sea creature with a land plant, all the way up, in order.
entities.longBio: The Kumulipo is a genealogical chant of about two thousand lines, composed for a chief born around 1700 and written down by King Kalakaua in 1889. It begins in darkness and moves through sixteen eras. The first thing born is the coral polyp, and after it come the sea creatures, each paired with a plant of the land, then the worms and shellfish, then fish, then insects, birds, reptiles, and eventually people - and the chiefly line runs on from there without a break. Reading it as a proto-evolutionary sequence has been popular and is probably too neat, but the order is genuinely from simple to complex.
entities.variantTraditions: Queen Liliuokalani translated it into English while imprisoned in Iolani Palace after the overthrow of 1893.

entities.name: The Menehune
entities.role: Small people who build enormous stonework in one night, and stop if anyone watches
epithets: the ones who work at night
entities.bio: The Menehune Ditch on Kauai is real, is beautifully cut, and nobody is sure who built it.
entities.longBio: The menehune are small people living in the forested uplands who are enormously skilled builders of stone and who work only at night and only in a single night, abandoning anything they cannot finish and vanishing if they are observed. They are credited with several genuine and impressive structures on Kauai, including the Alekoko fishpond and the Menehune Ditch, a dressed-stone watercourse whose construction technique is unlike other Hawaiian stonework. A suggestion that they were an earlier population is popular and unproven; an 1820 census of Kauai recorded sixty-five people as menehune.
entities.variantTraditions: The word may originally have meant something like commoner or low-ranking rather than small, which would change the story considerably.

entities.name: The Moo
entities.role: Lizard women who guard fresh water, and who are why you do not swim in some pools
symbols: the beautiful woman by the water
entities.abode: Fishponds, pools and stretches of fresh water
entities.bio: A pool with no ripple and a strangely still surface is one you leave alone.
entities.longBio: Moo are lizard beings, usually female, associated with fresh water - ponds, pools, fishponds, springs - which they own and guard. They appear as women or as enormous black lizards, and they are family guardians for some lineages and dangerous to everyone else. Signs of one include a pool that stays unnaturally still, and the appropriate response is to leave. Hiiaka fought a great many of them on her journey. They belong to a Pacific-wide association of reptiles with water, and they attach to specific named locations rather than being a general kind of creature.
entities.variantTraditions: Individual moo have names and places, and several are still identified with particular ponds on Oahu and Maui.

entities.name: Ta'aroa
entities.role: He sat alone inside a shell in the dark, and when he broke it he used the pieces for the sky
domains: the making of everything out of himself
symbols: the two shells, one becoming the sky and one the ground
entities.abode: Inside the shell, and then everywhere
entities.bio: There was nothing at all except him in an egg, and he had to make the world out of his own body.
entities.longBio: The Tahitian creation is the most austere in the Pacific. Ta'aroa existed alone inside a shell, rolling in the void, with no sky, no land, no sea and nobody to call to. He broke out. He used one half of the shell to make the sky and the other for the ground and the rocks. Then, having no other material, he made everything else out of himself: his feathers became the trees, his flesh the soil, his bones the mountains, his blood the redness of the sky and the rainbow. Other gods were then made and put to work. The whole account is about there having been nothing to work with.
entities.variantTraditions: Recorded by Teuira Henry from her missionary grandfather's manuscripts. The same god is the sea in Aotearoa - the divergence is the point.

entities.name: Oro
entities.role: War, and the god the Arioi society travelled the islands performing for
epithets: Oro-i-te-maro-tea, Oro of the yellow girdle
symbols: the to'o, a wrapped and bound image
entities.abode: Raiatea, and the great marae at Taputapuatea
entities.bio: His image was not a statue but a wrapped bundle of sennit, and the wrapping was the sacred part.
entities.longBio: Oro rose to dominance in the Society Islands in the centuries before contact, displacing Ta'aroa in practice, and his great marae at Taputapuatea on Raiatea was the ritual centre for a large part of eastern Polynesia - canoes came to it from as far as Aotearoa and Hawaii. His images, to'o, were not carved figures but pieces of wood wrapped in braided sennit, with the sacredness in the binding rather than the shape. His Arioi society was a travelling order of performers of high status with strict rules of membership, and it is one of the most distinctive institutions in the Pacific.
entities.variantTraditions: Taputapuatea is a UNESCO World Heritage site and voyaging canoes still call at it.

entities.name: Hiro
entities.role: A navigator and a thief, and rather good at both
entities.abode: Raiatea and the sea between the islands
entities.bio: He is a patron of thieves and of sailors, which in the old Pacific was not a strange pairing.
entities.longBio: Hiro is a navigator, a canoe-builder and a famous thief, and he is not embarrassed about any of it. He appears across eastern Polynesia - as Hiro in Tahiti and the Tuamotus, Whiro in Aotearoa, where he is considerably darker and becomes associated with evil and disease. The Tahitian Hiro is much closer to a folk hero: quick, capable, dishonest in an entertaining way, and formidable at sea. That the same name is a clever rogue in one archipelago and a malevolent power in another is the kind of divergence this pack exists to show.
entities.variantTraditions: Whiro in Maori tradition is a substantially different and more sinister figure and should not be read back into the Tahitian one.

entities.name: Tagaloa
entities.role: He stood in the empty sky and threw down a rock to have somewhere to put his feet
symbols: the rock thrown down into the sea
entities.bio: The first people came out of a rotting vine, which is not a flattering origin and is told anyway.
entities.longBio: Tagaloa existed in the sky when there was only sea below, and he threw down a rock to stand on, and that was the first land. He sent down a creeping vine to give shade. The vine grew, withered and rotted, and maggots bred in it, and Tagaloa sent his messenger to split them and give them limbs and hearts and minds, and they were the first people. Samoan tradition is precise about which rocks and which islands. The Tongan Tangaloa is a related figure whose descendants are the Tui Tonga line, which makes him ancestral to a real and long-lasting dynasty.
entities.variantTraditions: Samoan and Tongan accounts differ on how the islands were made and on the relation between Tagaloa and the chiefly lines.

entities.name: Nafanua
entities.role: A war goddess who fought with her chest bound, and stopped when the wind exposed her
symbols: four war clubs, each with its own name
the ti leaves binding her chest
entities.abode: Falealupo, at the western end of Savaii
entities.bio: Her father gave her four named clubs and told her not to go too far, and she did not.
entities.longBio: Nafanua was born of a union between the underworld and a woman, was abandoned, and was raised by her father Saveasiuleo, who armed her with four war clubs each with its own name and sent her to free the people of Falealupo, who were being made to climb coconut trees upside down. She fought with her chest bound flat and was taken for a man until the wind lifted her covering in battle and the enemy saw and were dismayed. She stopped short of total conquest when told to, and afterwards distributed the chiefly titles. She is a real presence in Samoan politics and genealogy rather than only in stories.
entities.variantTraditions: Her prophecy to Malietoa Fitisemanu that a kingdom would come from heaven was later read by missionaries as predicting Christianity.

entities.name: Sina and the Eel
entities.role: An eel fell in love with her, was killed, and asked her to bury its head
symbols: the three marks on the coconut
entities.bio: That is why a coconut has a face on it - two eyes and a mouth - and why you drink through it.
entities.longBio: Sina kept a small eel as a pet and it grew large and it turned out to be a young chief under an enchantment, and it began to follow her and to look at her in a way she did not want. She fled from pool to pool across the islands and it followed. Eventually it was caught and killed, and its last request was that its head be buried, and she did it. From the buried head grew the first coconut palm. The husked nut has three marks on it, two eyes and a mouth, and when you drink from it you put your mouth to the eel's, which is the punchline the whole story exists for.
entities.variantTraditions: Told in Samoa, Tonga and Fiji with local variation. The face on the nut is the constant.

entities.name: Hikuleo
entities.role: The ruler of Pulotu, the land of the dead, kept on a leash by two brothers
epithets: the one with the long tail
symbols: the rope held at both ends
entities.bio: Tangaloa held one end of the rope in the sky and Maui the other underground, so she could not take everything.
entities.longBio: Hikuleo rules Pulotu, the land of the dead, and claimed the firstborn of everything that grew or was born - which if allowed to continue would have emptied the world. Tangaloa above and Maui below therefore put a rope around Hikuleo, one holding it in the sky and the other in the underworld, so that the range of the claim is limited. The gender varies between accounts, male in some and female in others, and Hikuleo has a long tail. Pulotu itself is a real place-name argument: it may preserve the memory of an actual island of origin in the west.
entities.variantTraditions: Tongan and Samoan versions differ on gender and on which brothers hold the rope.

entities.name: Maui-kisikisi
entities.role: The Tongan Maui, who fished up the islands and brought fire, and does not die
entities.bio: In Tonga there are three Maui in a line - grandfather, father and son - and this is the son.
entities.longBio: Tongan tradition has three generations of Maui: Maui-motua, Maui-atalanga and Maui-kisikisi, the youngest, who is the trickster. He got the great hook from an old man in the underworld, went out with his brothers, hooked the sea floor and hauled up Tongatapu and the other islands, and the line broke before he could bring the whole thing to the surface. He also stole fire from the underworld, was burned, and the burns are why some trees hold fire in them and can be used to make it. He is not killed here. The Maori ending, where Maui dies attempting the goddess of death, is not part of the Tongan telling.
entities.variantTraditions: The three-generation Maui line is specifically Tongan; elsewhere he is a single figure with brothers.

entities.name: Make-make
entities.role: The chief god of Rapa Nui, and his face is carved everywhere at Orongo
epithets: the god of the birdman cult
symbols: the large-eyed face carved in rock
entities.abode: Rapa Nui, and the cliffs at Orongo
entities.bio: He is the one who made people, and his face - huge eyes, beaked mouth - is cut into the rock in hundreds.
entities.longBio: Make-make is the principal god of Rapa Nui and the creator of people, and his face is the most repeated image on the island after the moai: a mask with enormous eyes and a beaked mouth, carved into the rock at Orongo in very large numbers. He is bound up with seabirds and with the egg, and it is his cult that the birdman competition served. Rapa Nui is the most isolated inhabited place in the world - some 3,500 kilometres from the nearest continent and 2,000 from the nearest inhabited island - and the tradition there developed further from the rest of Polynesia than any other.
entities.variantTraditions: The relation between Make-make and the earlier ancestor cult of the moai is not fully understood; the birdman cult appears to be later.

entities.name: Hotu Matu'a
entities.role: The first settler, who came because his navigator had dreamed the island
entities.bio: A priest dreamed of the island, seven scouts were sent to find it, and it was there.
entities.longBio: Hotu Matu'a came from a homeland called Hiva, defeated or displaced, and made the voyage in two large canoes with his household. The tradition says a priest dreamed of the island and seven scouts were sent ahead to find it and prepare, and that they landed at Anakena. His sons founded the lineages that divided the island between them, and the whole later history of Rapa Nui - the moai, the clan territories, the collapse and the birdman cult - runs from that division. To find a speck of land that size at that distance, on purpose, is the single most impressive act of navigation in human history.
entities.variantTraditions: The seven scouts are commemorated by the seven moai at Ahu Akivi, which unusually face out to sea.

entities.name: The Birdman
entities.role: An annual competition to fetch the first sooty tern egg, and the winner ruled for a year
symbols: the first egg of the season
entities.abode: Orongo, and the islet of Motu Nui
entities.bio: Competitors' servants swam to an islet through shark water, waited for the egg, and swam back with it.
entities.longBio: Each spring the clans sent representatives - hopu, servants, not the competitors themselves - down the cliff at Orongo, into the sea, and out to the islet of Motu Nui, where they waited, sometimes for weeks, for the sooty terns to lay. The first to get an egg shouted the name of his sponsor across the water, swam back with the egg tied to his forehead, and climbed the cliff. His sponsor became tangata manu for the year, with considerable authority and severe restrictions. It replaced the older ancestor cult of the moai, ran into the nineteenth century, and ended with slave-raiding and missionisation in the 1860s.
entities.variantTraditions: The last recorded competition was around 1867. Some competitors died in the swim or on the cliff.
